Your gold and your silver are corroded, and their corrosion will be for a testimony against you, and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up your treasure in the last days. Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies. You have lived delicately on the earth, and taken your pleasure. You have nourished your hearts as in a day of slaughter. You have condemned, you have murdered the righteous one. He doesn’t resist you.

echoes.text: Wail; for the day of Yahweh is at hand! It will come as destruction from the Almighty.
echoes.note: 'Come now, you rich, weep and howl' opens with the prophetic woe-cry, 'Wail, for the day of the LORD is near.' The same howling-summons announces eschatological judgment on the complacent.

echoes.text: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come! Go to Calneh, and see; and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. are they better than these kingdoms? or is their border greater than your border? Those who put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; Who lie on beds of […]
echoes.note: Amos's woe on those 'at ease… who lie on beds of ivory and eat lambs from the flock' and 'are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph' is the prophetic template for James's denunciation of the luxurious rich who have 'lived delicately on the earth.' The coherence of theme and the day-of-slaughter motif are strong.

echoes.text: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates. In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to Yahweh, and it be sin to you.
echoes.note: 'You shall give him his wages… lest he cry against you to the LORD' is the law James indicts the rich for breaking: 'the wages of the laborers you kept back by fraud cry out.' The crying-out-to-God of withheld wages is verbally and legally precise.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
echoes.note: 'The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning' is the Holiness-Code companion to Deuteronomy 24, prohibiting exactly the withholding James condemns.

echoes.text: I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against the perjurers, and against those who oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and who deprive the foreigner of justice, and don’t fear me,” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The LORD comes in judgment 'against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages,' a prophetic restatement of the offense and the cry that reaches God.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
echoes.note: 'The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground' is the archetype of injustice that cries out to God, behind 'the cries… have entered the ears of the Lord of Hosts.'

echoes.text: though I am decaying like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
echoes.note: 'Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten' contributes the corrosion-and-moth imagery of decaying wealth (cf. Isaiah 50:9; 51:8).

echoes.text: Let us oppress the righteous poor; Let us not spare the widow, Nor reverence the hairs of the old man gray for length of years. But let our strength be to us a law of righteousness; For that which is weak is found to be of no service. But let us lie in wait for the righteous man, Because he is of disservice to us, And is contrary to our works, And upbraids us with sins against the law, And lays to our charge sins against our discipline. He professes to […]
echoes.note: The wicked who 'oppress the righteous poor man' and resolve to 'condemn him to a shameful death' is the Second-Temple righteous-sufferer scene behind 'you have condemned, you have murdered the righteous one. He does not resist you.'

pericopes.text: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain. You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand. Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged. Behold, the judge stands at the door. Take, brothers, for an example of suffering and of patience, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

echoes.text: that I will give the rain of your land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain, your new wine, and your oil.
echoes.note: 'I will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain' is the covenant promise James invokes for the patient farmer who waits 'until it receives the early and late rain.' The early/late-rain pair is distinctive.

echoes.text: “Be glad then, you children of Zion, and rejoice in Yahweh, your God; for he gives you the former rain in just measure, and he causes the rain to come down for you, the former rain and the latter rain, as before.
echoes.note: 'He has given the early rain… the early and the latter rain' restates the same agricultural promise as a sign of restoration, reinforcing the patient-farmer figure.

echoes.text: Neither do they say in their heart, ‘Let us now fear Yahweh our God, who gives rain, both the former and the latter, in its season; who preserves to us the appointed weeks of the harvest.’
echoes.note: 'Let us fear the LORD… who gives the rain in its season, the autumn and the spring rains' supplies a further early/late-rain antecedent.

echoes.text: He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name.” In all this, Job did not sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing.
echoes.note: 'You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and seen the outcome of the Lord' depends on the Job narrative — his endurance under loss without sin, and the restored 'outcome' of Job 42. James makes Job the type of patient endurance.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: 'How the Lord is full of compassion and mercy' reproduces the LORD's self-revelation, 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love' — the formula echoed across the Psalter (103:8; 111:4).

pericopes.text: But above all things, my brothers, don’t swear, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath; but let your “yes” be “yes”, and your “no”, “no”; so that you don’t fall into hypocrisy.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Do not swear… let your yes be yes' rests on 'you shall not swear by my name falsely,' the Holiness-Code regulation of oaths that James radicalizes into avoiding oaths altogether.

echoes.text: When you vow a vow to Yahweh your God, you shall not be slack to pay it; for Yahweh your God will surely require it of you; and it would be sin in you. But if you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you. You shall observe and do that which has gone out of your lips. Whatever you have vowed to Yahweh your God as a freewill offering, which you have promised with your mouth, you must do.
echoes.note: The law on vows — that one must perform what is sworn and that refraining from vowing is no sin — is the legal background to James's counsel against swearing.

echoes.text: Accustom not your mouth to an oath; And be not accustomed to the naming of the Holy One. For as a servant that is continually scourged will not lack a bruise, So he also that swears and names God continually will not be cleansed from sin. A man of many oaths will be filled with iniquity; And the scourge will not depart from his house: If he shall offend, his sin will be upon him; And if he disregard it, he has sinned doubly; And if he has sworn in vain, […]
echoes.note: 'Do not accustom your mouth to oaths… a man who swears many oaths is full of iniquity' is the wisdom counsel against swearing that most closely parallels James.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest?
echoes.note: 'Heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool' grounds the prohibition of swearing 'by heaven or by earth,' since both belong to God.

pericopes.text: Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises. Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord, and the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven. Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective. Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it didn’t rain on the earth for three years and six months. He prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.

echoes.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
echoes.note: 'Elijah… prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it did not rain' draws directly on Elijah's word that 'there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.' James reads the drought as answered prayer.

echoes.text: Elijah said to Ahab, “Get up, eat and drink; for there is the sound of abundance of rain.” So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he bowed himself down on the earth, and put his face between his knees. He said to his servant, “Go up now, look toward the sea.” He went up, and looked, and said, “There is nothing.” He said, “Go again” seven times. On the seventh time, he said, “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, […]
echoes.note: 'He prayed again, and the sky gave rain' depends on Elijah on Carmel bowing to the ground in prayer until the rain came. The two-part drought-and-rain narrative is the backbone of James's example of the righteous person's prayer.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.
echoes.note: 'The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous, and his ears toward their cry' grounds 'the insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.'

echoes.text: The sacrifice made by the wicked is an abomination to Yahweh, but the prayer of the upright is his delight.
echoes.note: 'The prayer of the upright is acceptable to him' (cf. 15:29, 'he hears the prayer of the righteous') is the proverbial basis for the efficacy of the righteous person's prayer.

echoes.text: Also there arose Elijah the prophet as fire, And his word burned like a torch: Who brought a famine upon them, And by his zeal made them few in number. By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven: Thrice did he thus bring down fire.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's praise of Elijah, who 'shut up the heavens' and 'brought down fire,' is the Second-Temple reception of the drought-prayer that James presupposes.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: 'Love covers all offenses' stands behind 'he who turns a sinner… will cover a multitude of sins,' the proverb of love covering sin applied to restoring the wanderer.

echoes.text: When I tell the wicked, O wicked man, you shall surely die, and you don’t speak to warn the wicked from his way; that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood will I require at your hand. Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.
echoes.note: The watchman who warns the wicked to turn 'will have saved his life' is the prophetic logic behind saving a soul from death by turning the sinner back (cf. Ezekiel 3:18-21).

echoes.text: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'Those who turn many to righteousness' shine like the stars — a faint echo behind turning a sinner from the error of his way.
